{"id":"PKIX-77k9.4","title":"Rust TLS ecosystem integration: rustls, ring, reqwest","description":"Create integration crates that let the existing Rust TLS ecosystem use PKIX as the certificate verifier. Without this, PKIX is a better engine that nobody can install in their car.

Deliverables:
1. pkix-rustls-provider: impl rustls::crypto::CryptoProvider or rustls::ServerCertVerifier backed by pkix-chain + DefaultVerifier. This is the highest-impact integration — rustls is the dominant Rust TLS library.
2. pkix-ring-verifier: impl SignatureVerifier backed by ring (for callers who want ring's asm-optimized crypto instead of RustCrypto).
3. Example: reqwest + pkix-rustls-provider working end-to-end.
4. Example: hyper + pkix-rustls-provider working end-to-end.

Approach: We may need to PR upstream to rustls to expose the right extension points, or work with the rustls ServerCertVerifier trait as-is. Research required.

May also want: pkix-wolfcrypt-verifier as the FIPS story (wolfSSL's own product).

Acceptance: A reqwest HTTPS client validates a real TLS connection using PKIX path validation + system trust store, with no rustls-webpki in the dep tree.","status":"open","priority":1,"issue_type":"epic","owner":"mark@wolfssl.com","created_at":"2026-06-15T19:45:48Z","created_by":"Mark Atwood","updated_at":"2026-06-15T19:45:48Z","metadata":{},"dependencies":[{"issue_id":"","depends_on_id":"PKIX-77k9","type":"parent-child","created_at":"2026-06-15T12:45:47Z","created_by":"Mark Atwood","metadata":"{}"}]}

{"notes":"Deliverable 1 of 4 is done: pkix-rustls 0.1.0 (unpublished) implements rustls::client::danger::ServerCertVerifier over pkix_chain::verify_tls_server. 9 tests drive the rustls trait itself; CI green on acf76d8b.

THE ACCEPTANCE CRITERION AS WRITTEN CANNOT BE MET. It asks for 'no rustls-webpki in the dep tree'. Verified against rustls 0.23.46's own manifest: rustls-webpki is an unconditional, non-optional dependency (package = "rustls-webpki", no optional = true), because rustls's crypto-provider API is built on webpki's signature-algorithm types — WebPkiSupportedAlgorithms is what verify_tls12_signature and verify_tls13_signature take. No choice of verifier can remove it.

What is achieved instead, and what the criterion should say: rustls-webpki performs no path validation, no name matching and no trust decision. It is reduced to rustls's internal algorithm plumbing. Removing it from the tree needs the upstream change this bead already anticipated ('We may need to PR upstream to rustls').

Research findings worth keeping, so the next person does not redo them:
  - rustls stable is 0.23.46 (MSRV 1.71); 0.24.0-dev.3 exists, so a breaking line is coming but unreleased. Pinned rustls = "0.23".
  - rustls-pki-types is deliberately 1.x: the vocabulary a verifier is handed (CertificateDer, ServerName, UnixTime) is stable independently of rustls, so churn exposure is one trait, not the whole surface.
  - default-features = false on rustls matters — the defaults pull in aws-lc-rs, and a consumer who chose ring should not compile a second provider because of us. The provider is passed in.
  - Install path: ClientConfig::builder_with_provider(p).with_safe_default_protocol_versions()?.dangerous().with_custom_certificate_verifier(Arc<dyn ServerCertVerifier>).
  - rustls_pki_types::ServerName is #[non_exhaustive]; an unrecognised variant must be refused, not passed through.

Scope decision: the trait's three jobs are the chain (ours), the TLS 1.2/1.3 handshake signatures (the peer proving key possession — delegated to the caller's CryptoProvider via rustls's own helpers) and the advertised schemes (also the provider's). Answering the latter two ourselves would mean becoming a crypto provider, which a PKI library should not be. The bead's alternative hook, rustls::crypto::CryptoProvider, is therefore the wrong one and should be dropped from the description.

Still open: deliverable 2 (pkix-ring-verifier — SignatureVerifier backed by ring) and deliverables 3 and 4 (reqwest and hyper examples, which need a live TLS connection and so are their own piece of work)."}

{"notes":"Follow-up to the note above: the handshake-signature half is now ours too, and the webpki situation is better than that note said.

rustls's verify_tls12_signature/verify_tls13_signature begin with webpki::EndEntityCert::try_from(cert) to extract the public key. So delegating to them — which the first version of pkix-rustls did — put TWO X.509 parsers on the same certificate: ours for the chain, webpki's for the handshake signature. The signature check is not a PKI question but the parsing is, which is the half the original scope decision missed.

Both methods are now implemented in pkix-rustls::handshake: x509-cert parses, pkix_path::SignatureVerifier verifies. With this verifier installed NO webpki code runs in the connection — its two live paths were the default verifier (not installed) and those helpers (not called). It remains linked, because the dependency is unconditional, and dead.

So the acceptance criterion should be reworded to something achievable and meaningful, e.g. 'no webpki code executes in a verified connection', which is now true and tested. 'Not in the dep tree' still needs the upstream change, but the argument for it is much stronger now that a working verifier needs none of it.

Three TLS-specific constraints an X.509 OID does not carry, all implemented and all mutation-verified:
  - Curve pinning. ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256 means P-256; the OID does not say. Dropping the check makes the p384-sha384 fixture verify under the P-256 scheme, because pkix-path takes the curve from the key. rustls refuses that, so omitting it would have been LooserThanWild.
  - PKCS#1 v1.5 refused in TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446 §4.2.3), permitted in 1.2, decided before any cryptography so the two failures stay distinct.
  - RSASSA-PSS parameters are hand-encoded (hash, MGF1 over the same hash, salt = hash length) because that is how pkix-path is told what to do. Pinned byte-for-byte against the signatureAlgorithm fields of OpenSSL-generated PSS certs; a one-byte salt change breaks both the comparison and real verification.

Testing approach worth reusing: a certificate is a signature over its own TBSCertificate made with the issuer's key, which is structurally the same as a handshake signature. So pkix-path/tests/fixtures/sigalgs supplies real signatures and real keys with no TLS stack and no private key material. ECDSA P-256/P-384, Ed25519 and RSA-PSS SHA-256/SHA-512 all verify, each re-checked with a flipped byte.

API consequences: DigitallySignedStruct::new is pub(crate), so handshake::verify takes (scheme, signature) and the trait methods destructure — otherwise it could not be tested against a real signature. And the CryptoProvider is gone from PkixServerCertVerifier entirely: nothing deferred to rustls's crypto any more, so PkixServerCertVerifier::new(anchors) takes one argument and the 'pass the same provider the ClientConfig used' footgun is gone. supported_verify_schemes reports what this crate verifies, which is not the provider's list — ring has no ECDSA_NISTP521_SHA512 and pkix-path does.

CI green on ec70b4f2, all six jobs."}
